The model

Two questions, four regimes, one holding

Growth and inflation explain a large share of sector leadership. Cross them and you get four macro regimes; the Compass holds the single liquid exposure that fits each. Everything is evaluated on the last trading day of the month and held through the following month.

XLE = Energy, XLK = Technology, XLU = Utilities, XLP = Consumer Staples, IEF = 7–10y US Treasuries (XLP + IEF held 50/50)

The confirming inflation indicator

Inflation direction is read two ways at once — from the bond market's own forecast, and from what inflation-sensitive sectors are doing relative to defensive ones.

Positive basket = 0.5·XLE + ⅙·XLI + ⅙·XLF + ⅙·XLB
Negative basket = ⅓·XLU + ⅓·XLV + ⅓·XLP
Indicator = cumulative growth of positive ÷ cumulative growth of negative

XLE = Energy, XLI = Industrials, XLF = Financials, XLB = Materials, XLU = Utilities, XLV = Health Care, XLP = Consumer Staples

The four conditions, checked at month-end

  1. Growth up — SPY above its 200-day simple moving average.
  2. Level — the 5-year breakeven (T5YIE) above 2.0%, the Fed's target.
  3. Breakeven momentum — T5YIE higher than 60 trading days ago.
  4. Asset momentum — the slope of a 60-day linear regression on the indicator is positive.
Inflation-on = Level AND ( Breakeven momentum OR Asset momentum )

The two momentum tests share a 60-day window but use different estimators on purpose: a point-to-point change is the natural read on the breakeven, while a regression slope is the noise-robust read on the choppier sector ratio. The OR only ever moves the model into energy earlier.

Does the replication hold?

Varadi publishes enough detail to check the rebuild rather than trust it. Occupancy — how much time the model spends in each holding — is the sharpest test, since it depends on every condition being right and nothing else.

Implementation

What it takes to actually run this

Everything above assumes the signal is read and traded at the same close. Three things decide whether that survives contact with a real account: when the data is knowable, when the trade is filled, and how often you look.

When the data is knowable

Two different lags get conflated here — when the data is knowable, and when the trade is filled. They are independent, and only one of them is forced on you.

The breakeven is published after the close. FRED stamps T5YIE for day D with a last-updated time of roughly 17:00 ET on D — an hour after the bell. So T5YIE(D) genuinely is not knowable when you trade the close of D. That much is a hard constraint.

But it costs a day of data, not a day of execution. Yesterday's print is in hand long before today's close, so you compute the signal during the session and send a market-on-close order. The realistic baseline is therefore T5YIE(D−1) filled at the close of D — the highlighted cell below. Deferring the fill to D+1 is a choice about when you run the job, not something the data imposes.

Breakeven used at the close of D Fill at close D Fill at close D+1
T5YIE(D) — needs a live estimate 22.2% · $115 20.5% · $83
T5YIE(D−1) — yesterday's published print 20.7% · $86 19.1% · $63

CAGR and growth of $1, net of costs. The highlighted cell is the easy baseline — yesterday's print, filled market-on-close today, no lookahead anywhere. The bottom-right applies only if you also defer the fill by a session.

Lag 0 is recoverable. Nominal and TIPS yields quote live all session, so a real-time 5-year breakeven estimate at 15:45 puts you back in the top-left cell and is worth 1.5 points of CAGR over waiting for the print. Your estimate will differ from FRED's by a basis point or two, which is immaterial except when the level is sitting on the 2% threshold — where it decides the regime outright. That, rather than the fill, is the part worth engineering carefully.

One diagnostic worth noting: stepping the breakeven back a second day costs almost nothing further (20.7% to 20.6%). The damage is concentrated entirely in the first day, which is the signature of a lookahead being removed rather than a signal decaying.

Execution lag — how quickly the edge decays

Holding the data question aside, this is the fill question alone: the signal is computed from the close of the last trading day of each month, and a lag of N means the trade is filled at the close N trading days later, with the portfolio holding its previous position until then.

Net of 10bps per unit of turnover, on the headline breakeven basis so the top row ties to the figures above. Waiting 15 trading days costs 5.1 points of CAGR and takes the growth of $1 from $115 to $42. Varadi reports 4.8 points lost at one day; this build loses 1.7. Either way the decay is steep enough that month-end fills are a real implementation risk, not a rounding error.

Rebalance frequency — monthly, weekly, daily

The model specifies a month-end decision. Checking the same four conditions more often is the obvious thing to try, and it makes the strategy worse. All three lines below use identical rules and the implementable breakeven (yesterday's print, filled at today's close) — only the review cadence differs.

CadenceCAGR vs monthlySharpe Max drawdownChanges / yr Growth of $1
Monthlythe model as specified20.7%—1.10-17.6%3.3$86
Weeklyre-checked every Friday close17.5%-3.2 pts0.93-24.1%6.6$46
Dailyre-checked every trading day18.3%-2.4 pts0.95-22.0%12.2$53

Monthly wins on every measure: 20.7% against 17.5% weekly and 18.3% daily, with the shallowest drawdown and a third of the trading. Looking more often turns the same signal into 12 position changes a year against 3, and the extra activity is whipsaw, not edge — the month-end cadence is doing real work as a noise filter, not just saving costs.

Assets conditioned on the regime

What each regime has actually meant for assets the model does not trade. The regime is the one identified at the close of the previous month — the same information the strategy acts on, so nothing here is hindsight.

Each line is the growth of $1 held in the asset only during months governed by that regime, and in cash the rest of the time. The four lines therefore partition the sample exactly: multiplying their final values together reproduces buy-and-hold over the same months.

Worked example of the timing, from the end of the data: the reading taken 31 August 2026 was Reflation, so September 2026's return is credited to Reflation. The Reflation reading taken 25 September 2026 governs October 2026, which has not finished, so it appears nowhere on these charts yet.

Method, data, and caveats

Prices are Yahoo Finance daily closes, dividend-adjusted, so every figure is total return. The breakeven is FRED series T5YIE, forward-filled across its own holidays by at most five days. Sharpe and Sortino are excess of 3-month T-bills (FRED DTB3).

The simulation is daily. Signals are read at the month-end close and traded at that same close; between rebalances the book drifts with the market, and turnover is charged on the gap between the drifted book and the new target. Costs are 10bps per unit of turnover.

The window starts in 2003 because T5YIE begins 2003-01-02 and IEF launched in July 2002. Allocate Smartly runs to 1990 using a proxy for the breakeven; this build does not, so there is no pre-2003 out-of-sample period here.

T5YIE is published after the close. FRED's last-updated stamp for day D is around 17:00 ET on D, so the headline figures assume you estimate the breakeven from live nominal and TIPS quotes rather than read the print. The script exposes this as --bei-pub-lag; setting it to 1 substitutes yesterday's print and takes the CAGR from 22.2% to 20.7%. Varadi's published results, and therefore the validation table above, use the same-day value.

Execution timing matters more than parameters. Varadi reports that delaying every trade by one full trading day costs 4.8 points of CAGR; this build loses 1.7 points on the same test, with Sharpe falling to 1.12. Either way, some of the edge lives near the month-end transition — treat month-end fills as a real implementation risk.

The "Enhanced" grid is not Varadi's. Allocate Smartly describes parameter diversification but does not publish the settings they average over; the 12-set grid here is a reasonable stand-in, not a replication.

This is a concentrated, single-position strategy with real tracking error and few genuine stagflations in the sample. Reported results demonstrate the regime logic; they are not a projection.
